title: What product designers can learn from McKinsey and Toyota

Alesia Korenchuk Product designer working on complex B2B products. Curious about design, technology, AI, and better ways to make sense of complicated things. Product Design Design Thinking UX Design Problem Solving Product Management What product designers can learn from McKinsey and Toyota Alesia Korenchuk 5 min read · Oct 3, 2026 -- Listen Share Three frameworks for thinking more clearly about product problems, root causes, and design decisions. Press enter or click to view image in full size Everyone seems to be writing about AI right now. New AI skills. MCP. Better prompts. How to make Claude more efficient. What to do with your life while waiting for the limits to reset. All useful things. So naturally, I decided to write about frameworks that are decades old. Hear me out. The tools have changed dramatically. But some of the questions we deal with in product design haven’t: What problem are we actually solving? Are we solving the root cause or just treating a symptom? And how do we turn everything we know into a clear decision? Management consultants have spent decades learning how to structure messy problems and communicate complicated decisions. Toyota became famous for repeatedly asking one extremely simple question: “Why?” Which made me wonder: what happens if we steal a few of their tools? So I picked three: the Minto Pyramid, MECE, and the 5 Whys. None of them were created for product designers. All three are surprisingly useful for product design. Let’s see why. The Minto Pyramid: start with the point Let’s start with Barbara Minto. In 1963, she joined McKinsey after Harvard Business School, becoming the firm’s first female MBA professional hire. While working with consultants’ reports, she ran into a problem that still feels familiar: having good ideas doesn’t automatically make them easy to understand. As she worked on structuring those reports, the same pattern kept appearing: a pyramid. The logic is simple: one main point at the top, supporting ideas underneath, and details and evidence below. The further down you go, the more detail you get. Press enter or click to view image in full size And this feels surprisingly familiar in product design. You can have user feedback, analytics, technical constraints, three Figma pages and a very strong opinion about a dropdown. Having information is rarely the problem. Making a clear point out of all of it can be. Let’s take a completely fictional example. Imagine we’re redesigning a sign-up flow and, after looking at the data and user feedback, we decide: We should simplify the sign-up form. That’s the top of the pyramid. Underneath come the reasons: users drop off before completing it, some fields aren’t actually needed at sign-up, and users can provide the rest later. And below that comes the evidence: analytics, user feedback, and research. That’s it. Instead of starting with everything you found and slowly working your way toward the conclusion, you flip it: Point first. Reasoning underneath. Details when needed. MECE: no overlaps, no gaps MECE stands for Mutually Exclusive, Collectively Exhaustive . Barbara Minto coined the acronym at McKinsey, and despite the slightly intimidating name, the idea is pretty simple: No overlaps. No gaps. Let’s forget product design for a minute and imagine we’re organizing a wardrobe. You create four categories: Trousers, Summer clothes, Black clothes, and Nike. Looks organized. Until you pick up a pair of black Nike shorts . Where do they go? They’re summer clothes. They’re black. They’re Nike. And depending on how generous we are with the definition of trousers, we might have even more problems. That’s the problem: our boxes overlap. A better way would be to choose one rule. If we organize everything by type, for example, we could have Tops, Bottoms, Dresses, and Outerwear. Now our shorts have a home: Bottoms. Same logic. No overlaps. No gaps. Press enter or click to view image in full size Now back to product design. Imagine you have 50 pieces of user feedback after a release: slow loading, confusing terminology, missing functionality, something users can’t find, and the inevitable “it doesn’t work.” You start putting similar feedback together and end up with groups like Performance, Comprehension, Navigation, and Functionality. Then you do the same MECE check: Do these categories overlap? Is anything important left out? MECE doesn’t tell you what your categories should be. They depend on the problem you’re looking at. It simply helps you check whether the structure you created makes sense. And once the mess starts looking like a pattern, there’s another question: Why is this happening? Which brings us to Toyota. The 5 Whys: don’t stop at the symptom The 5 Whys became part of Toyota’s approach to problem solving and continuous improvement. The idea is almost suspiciously simple: when something goes wrong, don’t just fix what you can see. Keep asking: Why? And then ask it again. The goal is to get past the symptom and closer to the root cause . At Toyota, when a problem occurs in production, simply fixing the immediate issue isn’t necessarily enough. The goal is to understand why it happened in the first place and prevent it from happening again. Fix the symptom, and the problem may come back. Find the cause, and you have a chance to prevent it. Press enter or click to view image in full size And no, there’s nothing magical about the number five. Sometimes three Whys are enough. Sometimes you need more.
